patterns.title: Threshold Contribution Problems
patterns.domain: Strategic and game-theoretic problems; threshold public goods and conditional commitments

sources.title: Van de Kragt, Orbell, and Dawes, The Minimal Contributing Set as a Solution to Public Goods Problems (1983)
sources.supports: Early fixed-contribution threshold experiments, minimal contributing set, communication and coalition designation.
sources.boundary: Publisher abstract read. No unverified sample details, effect sizes, or universal causal claim are added. The paper proposes criticalness as an explanation; the article does not treat that proposed mechanism as demonstrated for the hypothetical backers.

sources.title: Bagnoli and Lipman, Provision of Public Goods: Fully Implementing the Core through Private Contributions (1989)
sources.supports: Refund-on-failure mechanism; complete information and flexible contribution assumptions; distinction between ordinary Nash and undominated perfect equilibrium.
sources.read_method: Author-hosted published PDF downloaded and extracted locally. Introduction, formal definitions, single-unit mechanism, and discussion of inefficient Nash equilibria read.
sources.boundary: The theorem uses a different contribution space and stronger equilibrium selection than the binary backer example. No guaranteed provision or elimination of all ordinary Nash failure equilibria is claimed.

sources.title: List and Lucking-Reiley, The Effects of Seed Money and Refunds on Charitable Giving (2002)
sources.supports: Published field experiment, random assignment of 3,000 households to six fundraising treatments; effects of seed money and refunds; two of three refund campaigns below target and donations returned.
sources.read_method: Published PDF read, including methods, solicitation terms, and results. Author version also inspected; article links the published version.
sources.boundary: Selected prospective donors in one university capital campaign. Raising more donations does not establish net profitability or predict hypothetical backer behavior; preparation and solicitation costs matter.

sources.title: Kickstarter, Creator Handbook: Funding
sources.supports: Official all-or-nothing model: below-goal campaigns do not collect pledges; creators should budget for the promised delivery and rewards.
sources.read_method: Official handbook opened and read in this conversation, including funding model, budget, and support guidance.
sources.boundary: Does not establish Maya’s extra full-collection or shortfall-return conditions, a public-good structure for all campaigns, guaranteed payment collection, or delivery.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when a shared project needs a minimum combined contribution, then distinguish protecting pledges from coordinating enough contributors to make provision possible.
use_when: What has to happen before an all-or-nothing film can proceed?
Maya crowdfunds a free-to-watch documentary. Ari, Bea, and Cam’s agreed shares are jointly sufficient; Dev can benefit without paying.
goals: Recognize the familiar predicament before specialist terminology.
Explain the defining mechanism and distinguish neighboring concepts.

Binary complete-information teaching benchmark separated from the campaign’s practical procedure. Refund protection and coordination are distinct; no-contribution can remain a weak equilibrium when an unsuccessful isolated pledge is costless. Kickstarter supports only the documented all-or-nothing rule, not this campaign’s extra guarantees.
Separate hypothetical behavior, model results, documented cases, and practical editorial proposals.
mechanisms: Collect only after valid sufficient pledges; authorize production only after actual sufficient collection; use the expressly agreed shortfall-return rule.
Payment failures, production risk, unequal contributions, and administration remain. These extra conditions are not attributed to every platform.
example_user_queries: What has to happen before an all-or-nothing film can proceed?

visual.question: What has to happen before an all-or-nothing film can proceed?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Ari, Bea, and Cam’s agreed pledges are all required in this plan for Maya’s free-to-watch film. Valid sufficient pledges permit collection; only sufficient actual collection permits production. A missing pledge blocks collection; a shortfall triggers this hypothetical campaign’s return rule. Dev can watch without pledging. Change: Protect failed pledges, coordinate enough real backing, and check collected funds before production. Limitation: Payment failures, production risk, unequal contributions, and administration remain. These extra conditions are not attributed to every platform.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The crowdfunding example separates sufficient commitments, successful collection, and eventual production. All-or-nothing pledges address one failure risk; the hypothetical shortfall-return rule adds a separate protection. Funding does not guarantee completion, and preparation still needs coverage.
